scene.testo: May 1945. A team of American economists is sent to a castle on the Baltic coast. Inside is the man who ran Hitler's war production. They have one question. Of all the bombs dropped on Germany, which hurt most?
Albert Speer answered for days. But his clearest answer was not a city. It was not a factory. It was a single day in May 1944. And that answer came with two problems.
First, Germany kept fighting for almost a year after that day. Second, the man giving the answer was already working on the story that would save his life. So what did he actually say?

The place was Glucksburg Castle, near Flensburg, close to the Danish border. After Hitler's death, Admiral Doenitz set up the remains of the Nazi government nearby. Speer came with him. The Allies had not yet arrested them.
For a few days, a German minister sat in a northern town and explained his own defeat to the people who had caused it. The questioners came from the United States Strategic Bombing Survey.
Among them were Paul Nitze, who later shaped American Cold War strategy, George Ball, who later served at the State Department, and a young economist named John Kenneth Galbraith.

Their mission was simple. Find out what air power had really done to Germany before the evidence disappeared. And Speer was the best witness they could hope for. He knew every factory, every bottleneck, every number.

Speer had taken over armaments in February 1942. Under him, German war production kept rising year after year, even as the bombs fell. And he wanted to talk. But he was also thinking about his own future.
He told them about Hamburg. In July 1943, a week of British and American raids destroyed much of the city. Speer told the interrogators what he had said at the time, and it was dramatic.

He said he had told Hitler that if such attacks continued, they could bring a rapid end to the war. But the attacks did not continue that way. Hamburg recovered enough to work, and production kept climbing.

That was the pattern Speer kept describing. The Allies found a weak point, hit it hard, then moved on. Ball bearing plants. Aircraft factories. Each time, the Germans repaired, dispersed and kept producing.

So the Americans pressed him. Was there any attack Germany could not recover from? Speer's answer pointed to one industry. And at the moment he feared for it most, an American general in England was fighting for permission to strike it.

General Carl Spaatz commanded the American strategic bombers in Europe. For months he argued for one target. Germany's fuel. In the spring of 1944 he proposed the plan. Hit the synthetic fuel plants, and the army and air force would run dry.

But the invasion of France was coming. Eisenhower's planners wanted the bombers used against railways and bridges first. The oil plan was turned down. Spaatz kept pushing, and in April he won permission to try it for a few days.

Over central Germany that spring, the weather refused to cooperate. For weeks the bombers waited. Years later, Speer would put a date on what came next. And he wrote it down in a way no reader could miss.
He wrote that he would never forget the date of May 12. On that day, he said, the technological war was decided. So what happened on Friday, May 12, 1944?

Nearly 900 American heavy bombers flew deep into Germany. Their targets were not cities. They were synthetic fuel plants, where Germany turned coal into gasoline. Leuna, Bohlen, Zeitz, Luetzkendorf and Bruex.
Fewer than fifty bombers did not return. Leuna, near Merseburg, was the largest plant of all. Its towers, pipes and tanks filled the horizon. This was the heart of the German fuel supply.
The next day, Speer went there himself. With the plant's technicians, he picked his way through a tangle of broken, twisted pipes. He found that chemical plants were extremely sensitive to bombing.
A single day of attacks cut German aviation fuel output by more than one thousand tons a day. Production plunged. Every aircraft, every training flight and every tank column depended on those plants.
On May 19, Speer flew to the Obersalzberg and told Hitler what he had seen. Field Marshal Keitel was in the room. Speer said the enemy had struck one of the weakest points in German industry.

He warned that if the enemy kept it up, Germany would soon have no fuel production worth mentioning. Then he added one more line. Their only hope, he said, was that the other side had as scatterbrained an air staff as their own.

Keitel told Hitler they would survive this blow too. And for a few weeks, as the bombers turned to support the invasion of France, it looked as if Keitel was right. But this time, the Americans did not move on.
Allied codebreakers were reading German signals, and they saw the reaction. Orders to save fuel and protect the plants at almost any cost. The Germans were worried, and now the Allies knew it.
After D-Day, the attacks returned and kept coming. On June 30, Speer wrote to Hitler that the enemy had increased German aviation fuel losses to ninety percent by June 22.
In April, the synthetic plants produced 175,000 tons of aviation fuel. In July, 30,000. In September, 5,000. From May onward, Germany was using more fuel than it could make.
What followed was a race. A special commissioner, Edmund Geilenberg, was given up to 350,000 men, many of them forced laborers, to repair the plants and move what could be moved underground.
Each time Leuna came back into partial production, the bombers came back too. It was attacked twenty-two times. Over a full year, it averaged only nine percent of its capacity.
By December, the shortage showed on the Western Front. Pilot training, already cut, was reduced again for lack of aviation fuel. Panzer units found it harder and harder to move.
In the Ardennes that December, Germany launched its last great offensive in the West without enough fuel to finish it. Many tank units were simply abandoned when their tanks ran dry.

scene.testo: By the end of the year, Speer said the fuel shortage had become catastrophic. In March 1945, he warned Hitler that the German economy faced inevitable collapse within four to eight weeks.

So was Speer telling the truth? He was a gifted storyteller, and his best stories were about himself. At Nuremberg he presented himself as a technician who knew little of the regime's crimes. He escaped the gallows with twenty years in prison.

Historians have since shown how false that picture was. His famous memoirs were written in prison and published in 1969. So why trust this part? Because it does not rest on his memory. His reports to Hitler from 1944 survive.

The production figures survive too, and the Survey checked them plant by plant. One question remains. If one day decided it, why did the war last another year? Speer blamed a lack of continuity. The oil campaign came late, and not everyone believed in it. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command called it a panacea and kept sending most of his bombers against cities.

In 1945, the Americans went to that castle to ask which bombs mattered. They got hundreds of pages of answers. But the one people remember is a Friday in May 1944, when nearly 900 bombers went for fuel instead of cities.

descrizione:
In May 1945, American investigators questioned Albert Speer, Hitler's armaments minister, and asked which Allied bombing hurt Germany most. His answer pointed to one day: May 12, 1944, when American bombers struck Germany's synthetic fuel plants.

This documentary follows the interrogation at Glucksburg, the oil campaign pushed by General Carl Spaatz, Speer's warnings to Hitler, the collapse of German fuel output and the shortages that crippled the Luftwaffe and the panzers by December 1944. It also examines why Speer's testimony deserves caution.
